current_recheck.methodSummary: Contre-revue statique limitée aux quatre JSON pointés par formation-manifest.json:99-103, au rapport initial, au manifeste p0-p2 et aux chemins de rendu/progression demandés (LessonViewer.tsx, chapterProgress.ts, blockRegistry.ts, learningDesign.ts ; YouTubePlayer.tsx, checkpointGate.ts et SingleChoiceExercise.tsx relus comme dépendances directes). Chaque constat initial a été retrouvé par courseId/lesson/chapterId, puis confronté au JSON actuel et au code qui le rend. Statut strict : resolved_with_evidence seulement si le constat entier est corrigé et rendu prouvable ; documented_removal seulement avec trace dans le manifeste de retraits ; still_open si la déficience persiste ou si le retrait non tracé ne prouve pas une correction ; externally_unverifiable pour une propriété qui ne peut être établie dans les données/code disponibles. Les 12 vidéos ont reçu objectiveBefore, mais conservent toutes l’absence de durée, langue, questions, transcription et alternative ; elles restent donc ouvertes. Les quatre checkpoints hérités du cours 01 ont disparu, mais ce retrait n’est pas documenté pour cette formation et aucune équivalence n’est présente : ils restent ouverts, sans transformer une absence d’écran en correction. Score : 100 − (4 P0 × 8 + 12 P2 × 2 + 12 P3 × 1) = 32 ; une résolution prouvée ou un retrait documenté porte une pénalité nulle, tandis qu’un constat non vérifiable porterait la moitié de sa pénalité (aucun ici). Cette grille rend la sévérité initiale explicite et ne confère aucun crédit aux corrections partielles non closes.

issues.description: La vidéo « The AI Product Management Masterclass [Complete Course] » est une ressource obligatoire pour avancer, mais ses métadonnées ne fournissent ni objectif avant lecture, ni durée/langue, ni questions de réinvestissement, ni transcription ou alternative textuelle. Elle apparaît après le contenu textuel du chapitre. Le lecteur ne peut donc afficher aucun cadrage dédié ; un apprenant ne sait pas ce qu’il doit en retirer ni combien de temps prévoir. La qualité ou l’accessibilité externe de la vidéo n’est pas mise en cause ici.
issues.current_content: Titre: « The AI Product Management Masterclass [Complete Course] » ; URL YouTube déclarée ; objectiveBefore, durationSeconds, videoLanguage, questionsAfter, transcript et alternativeTextFr absents ; optional absent.
issues.proposed_content: Après visionnage éditorial de la vidéo, ajouter avant le lecteur un objectif relié au chapitre (« Pendant cette vidéo, repérez … »), sa durée et sa langue, une alternative textuelle ou transcription, ainsi qu’une à deux questions post-lecture. body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to spot high-value, high-feasibility AI use cases aligned to measurable business outcomes. 2) How to assess data readiness and model fit to reduce delivery risk. 3) How to prioritize opportunities using value, effort, and risk to build an evidence-backed roadmap.

body.en:
Start with outcomes: tie opportunities to OKRs/KPIs (e.g., conversion rate, cost-to-serve, time-to-resolution, risk loss). Map user and business “jobs to be done,” pain points, and moments of friction to quantify potential impact.

Classify opportunity archetypes—prediction (likelihood), ranking (ordering), extraction (structure), generation (content), recommendation (choice), and forecasting (time series). Prefer augmentation over full automation early to reduce risk and speed learning.

Evaluate data readiness: availability, coverage/volume, quality and bias, label definitions, freshness, privacy/compliance, governance, and access paths. Check feasibility constraints: latency, throughput, integration surfaces, cost per inference, monitoring needs, and safety/ethics (fairness, security, IP, toxicity).

Form a value hypothesis and success thresholds (e.g., “reduce average handle time by 15% with no CSAT drop”). Run fast de-risking tests: rule/heuristic baselines, offline prototypes, small human-in-the-loop pilots, and manual labeling sprints.

Prioritize with a value–feasibility matrix or ICE/RICE scoring to select near-term wins that prove value while informing longer-term bets. Plan for measurement and iteration from the start (telemetry, A/B tests, guardrails, fallback paths).

• Outcome-aligned opportunity selection: tie each idea to a clear, measurable KPI.
• Augmentation before automation: assist users first to learn quickly and reduce risk.
• Data readiness checklist: availability, quality, labels, bias, privacy, and access paths.
• Opportunity archetypes: prediction, ranking, extraction, generation, recommendation, forecasting.
• Prioritization frameworks: value–feasibility matrix, ICE/RICE scoring with explicit assumptions.

• Start from measurable outcomes and user jobs, not from models.
• Favor augmentation, small pilots, and strong baselines to de-risk quickly.
• Use data readiness checks and value–feasibility scoring to build a focused roadmap.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to identify high-value AI opportunities, assess feasibility, and prioritize a de-risked path to impact.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to frame AI problems around users, outcomes, and testable hypotheses. 2) How to define success metrics, constraints, and evaluation plans before modeling. 3) How to recognize and avoid common AI product anti-patterns that derail delivery and impact.

**Good framing converts vague asks into clear problem statements: who is the user, what decision or action must improve, in which context, by how much, under what constraints (latency, cost, safety)? Express assumptions and a falsifiable value hypothesis (what must be true for this to work). Define output metrics (e.g., precision, factuality, latency) and outcome metrics (e.g., conversion lift, time saved, risk avoided) plus guardrails (safety, fairness). Use templates: “As a [user] in [context], I need [capability] to achieve [outcome]. We believe [intervention] will move [metric] by [threshold] within [time]. We will know we are right when [success criteria].” Map the input→model→decision→action→outcome chain to ensure the model’s output actually changes behavior. Plan evaluation: offline tests with realistic data and baselines; online tests (A/B or phased rollout) with monitoring, feedback loops, and fallback behavior. Common anti-patterns: solution-first thinking (naming a model before the problem), boiling the ocean (over-broad scope and edge cases in v1), benchmark chasing over business value, ignoring non-ML baselines, proxy-metric misalignment, premature optimization of architecture, data fishing/p-hacking, neglecting safety/compliance, skipping change management and user training, and lack of clear exit or rollback criteria.**

title.en: Feasibility, data readiness and risk assessment

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to evaluate technical and data feasibility for AI ideas 2) How to assess data readiness using quality dimensions and Data Readiness Levels (DRL) 3) How to identify, prioritize, and mitigate risks across privacy, fairness, safety, and operations

**AI feasibility spans desirability, feasibility, and viability, with feasibility covering technical approach, data readiness, integration constraints, and compliance. Technical feasibility considers whether an appropriate model class exists (e.g., classifier, ranking, generative), expected accuracy, latency/throughput targets, compute footprint, and integration with existing systems. Data feasibility centers on availability, access, and quality: do you have sufficient volume and coverage; are labels available; are there gaps, drift, or sampling bias; do you have consent and lawful basis (e.g., GDPR/CCPA); and can you ensure security and governance (PII handling, lineage, retention)? Data Readiness Levels (DRL) provide a practical shorthand: Grade C (data accessible and discoverable), Grade B (data faithful—cleaned, documented, unbiased as feasible), Grade A (data in analysis-ready form with defined schema and labels). Assess data quality across accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, and validity; run profiling and small labeling pilots to expose failure modes early. Risk assessment evaluates likelihood and impact for categories such as privacy/security, safety, fairness/bias, explainability, regulatory, IP, operational, and reputational risks. Use a structured method (risk matrix; FMEA: failure modes, effects, and criticality; hazard analysis) to prioritize risks and define controls: data minimization, anonymization, encryption, differential privacy, access controls, consent management, DPIAs, bias audits, human-in-the-loop, rate limiting, content filters, red teaming, monitoring/alerts, rollback plans. Document assumptions and mitigations via artifacts like data sheets, model cards, and an ethics review. Gate progress with stage checks: (1) problem-value fit, (2) data readiness and baseline viability, (3) pilot and risk controls validated, (4) productionization plan including monitoring and incident response.**

• Data Readiness Levels (DRL): C=accessible, B=trustworthy/understood, A=analysis-ready with labels and documentation
• Feasibility checklist: problem framing, success criteria, model approach, data inventory/quality, latency/compute, integration, compliance
• Risk matrix and controls: prioritize by likelihood×impact; mitigate with privacy safeguards, bias testing, human-in-the-loop, guardrails, and monitoring

• Validate technical, data, legal, and operational feasibility early; stop or pivot when blockers persist
• Use DRL and data quality dimensions to determine if data is analysis-ready
• Prioritize risks with a matrix and apply concrete mitigations; document via data sheets, model cards, and DPIAs
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to assess feasibility, evaluate data readiness, and manage AI risks to move from idea to validated pilot.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to define outcome-oriented success metrics aligned to user value and business goals 2) How to connect model performance to product metrics and ROI 3) How to craft testable ROI hypotheses and validate them with experiments and guardrails

**Good AI metrics start from outcomes: choose a North Star (e.g., retention, revenue, cost-to-serve) and supporting metrics (engagement, quality, safety). Differentiate lagging (revenue, churn) from leading indicators (task success rate, time saved) to enable faster iteration. Map model metrics (accuracy, precision/recall, F1, AUC, calibration; MAE/RMSE for regression; latency and cost per inference; hallucination rate and helpfulness for generative) to product and business impact (conversion, deflection, activation, NPS/CSAT, AHT reduction). Define guardrails for quality, safety, and fairness to avoid harmful wins. An ROI hypothesis states expected benefit relative to cost: ROI = (Benefits − Costs) / Costs, with clear assumptions (traffic, adoption, baseline, uplift, price) and measurement windows. Include cost components: data acquisition/labeling, infra/training/inference, model/API/vendor fees, human review, compliance, maintenance/monitoring. Validate impact causally via A/B tests (or canary/shadow rollouts) with power analysis, MDE, and appropriate segmentation; use AA tests for instrumentation checks. For genAI, track answer correctness/usefulness, refusal/moderation rate, latency/TTFT, prompt-injection resilience, and human handoff. Set acceptance criteria and stop-loss thresholds before launch, and monitor post-release with leading metrics and alerts.**

• North Star and metric tree: outcome (e.g., cost-to-serve) with leading levers (deflection rate, task success, time saved)
• ROI hypothesis template: “We believe [change] will move [metric] by [X%] for [segment] because [insight]; we’ll know it worked when [leading indicator] and [guardrails] meet [criteria]”
• Experiment design: A/B or canary with power/MDE, guardrail metrics (quality, safety, fairness), and instrumentation/AA checks

• Tie AI success to user outcomes and business value, not just model scores
• Convert model performance to product metrics and ROI with explicit assumptions and cost accounting
• Validate causally via experiments with guardrails; set acceptance and stop-loss criteria before launch
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now define success metrics, craft ROI hypotheses, and design experiments to validate AI product impact.

As AI systems generate increasingly consequential outputs—medical summaries, legal drafts, financial recommendations—users need more than just an answer. They need to understand why the AI produced it, how certain it is, and where the information came from.

Explainability in UX does not mean exposing model internals. It means translating model reasoning into language and visuals that users can act on. A plain-language rationale ('This recommendation is based on your last 30 days of activity') is far more useful than a probability score.

Confidence indicators—such as color-coded reliability badges, hedging language ('likely', 'possibly'), or explicit percentage ranges—help users calibrate how much weight to give an AI output. However, poorly designed confidence UI can backfire: if users do not understand what '87% confident' means in context, the number adds noise rather than signal.

Citations and source links are critical for retrieval-augmented AI products. When an AI references a document, policy, or data source, linking directly to that source transforms the AI from an opaque oracle into a research assistant users can verify and trust.

No AI system is infallible. Designing for failure is not pessimism—it is professional responsibility. The quality of a fallback experience often determines whether a user abandons the product or remains a loyal advocate.

Fallback states occur when an AI cannot produce a useful output due to out-of-scope queries, low confidence, missing data, or policy constraints. Best-practice fallbacks are transparent ('I don't have enough information to answer this confidently'), constructive (offering alternative paths), and non-blaming (never making users feel they asked the wrong question).

Correction flows enable users to flag, edit, or reject AI outputs. A simple thumbs-down icon is insufficient; effective correction UI captures enough context for the system to learn and for the user to feel heard. Inline editing, structured feedback forms, and 'undo + explain' patterns are highly effective.

Human handoff is the most critical fallback of all. In customer service, healthcare triage, or legal tools, there are moments when only a human can help. The handoff UX must be seamless: carry over the conversation context, set wait-time expectations, and never make users repeat themselves to the human agent.

title.en: User Feedback Loops in AI Products

body.en:
A user feedback loop is a systematic process by which signals from users are captured, analyzed, and used to improve an AI product iteratively. In AI systems, feedback loops are especially powerful because they can directly influence model retraining, feature prioritization, and UX refinement.

Feedback can be explicit — such as ratings, thumbs up/down, or surveys — or implicit, derived from behavioral signals like click-through rates, session duration, or task abandonment. Effective loop design combines both types.

The loop consists of four stages: Collect (gather raw signals), Analyze (extract actionable insights), Act (implement changes to the model or product), and Validate (confirm improvement via metrics). Closing the loop means ensuring that user input visibly influences product behavior, which also builds user trust.

For AI products, special care must be taken to avoid feedback bias — when the system amplifies existing errors because it learns from its own flawed outputs. Diverse feedback sources and regular audits are essential safeguards.

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is a design paradigm where human judgment is embedded at critical points within an automated AI pipeline. Rather than fully autonomous decision-making, HITL ensures that humans review, correct, or approve AI outputs before they affect users or downstream systems.

HITL is essential in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, legal, and content moderation, where errors carry significant consequences. It also serves as a mechanism for generating labeled training data, catching model drift, and maintaining regulatory compliance.

Common HITL patterns include: Active Review (humans inspect every output), Threshold-Based Review (AI flags low-confidence outputs for human review), Sampling-Based Review (a random or stratified sample is reviewed periodically), and Adversarial Review (edge cases and failure modes are specifically targeted).

Designing effective HITL workflows requires clear role definition, efficient tooling for reviewers, calibration training to ensure reviewer consistency, and audit trails for accountability. The goal is not to slow down AI — but to make it reliably trustworthy.

Rigorous experimentation is how AI product teams separate genuine improvements from random noise. A/B testing — or controlled experiments — randomly assigns users to a control group (existing experience) and one or more treatment groups (new AI behavior) to measure causal impact.

For AI products, experiment design must account for unique challenges: model non-determinism, delayed feedback (e.g., recommendations whose value appears over days), novelty effects, and interference between users in social or recommendation systems.

Key elements of a well-designed AI experiment include: a clear hypothesis, a primary success metric aligned with user value, guardrail metrics to catch regressions, sufficient statistical power (sample size), a pre-defined runtime, and a holdout strategy.

Product analytics provides the measurement infrastructure — dashboards, funnels, cohort analyses, and event tracking — that feeds both experiments and ongoing monitoring. Metrics should be organized in a hierarchy: north star metric → product metrics → operational metrics. For AI specifically, tracking both outcome metrics (did users achieve their goal?) and model metrics (accuracy, latency, confidence distribution) is essential.

question.en: What is the primary purpose of guardrail metrics in an A/B experiment?

text.en: To replace the primary success metric if it proves difficult to measure
To detect unacceptable regressions in other dimensions while the primary metric improves
To increase the statistical power of the experiment
To determine the minimum sample size required for the experiment

explanation.en: Guardrail metrics act as safety nets. They ensure that while you are optimizing for your primary metric, you are not inadvertently degrading other critical dimensions of the product such as latency, error rates, or user retention.

question.en: Which of the following is a unique challenge of running A/B tests on AI-powered recommendation systems?

User interference, where recommendations for one user can influence the behavior of other users

A/B tests require a minimum of one million users to be statistically valid for AI products

title.en: Quality Thresholds for AI Product Launches

body.en:
Quality thresholds are pre-defined, measurable criteria that an AI product must meet before it is released to users. They transform the launch decision from a subjective judgment into an evidence-based process, reducing both the risk of shipping harmful products and the risk of delaying valuable ones unnecessarily.

Quality thresholds span multiple dimensions. Model quality includes accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and fairness metrics across demographic subgroups. Performance quality covers inference latency, system uptime, and error rates under production load. UX quality encompasses task completion rates, user satisfaction scores (CSAT, NPS), and error recovery success rates. Safety and ethical quality requires completing bias audits, adversarial testing, and privacy compliance reviews.

A practical launch readiness framework uses a tiered approach: mandatory thresholds (must-pass criteria — failure here blocks launch), advisory thresholds (important but waivable with documented rationale and a remediation plan), and monitoring commitments (metrics tracked post-launch with defined escalation triggers).

Post-launch, thresholds become the foundation of continuous monitoring — if metrics fall below defined baselines, automated alerts or rollback protocols are triggered. This transforms a one-time gate into an ongoing quality assurance system.

title.en: Training Users and Support Teams for AI Products

body.en:
Effective training is the bridge between a technically sound AI product and genuine user adoption. Training must be segmented by role: end users need task-focused guidance on interacting with AI outputs confidently and critically; power users need deeper understanding of model behavior and customization; support teams need to handle escalations, explain AI decisions in plain language, and triage edge cases.

Adult learning principles — relevance, immediate applicability, and feedback loops — should shape all training design. Scenario-based learning, where users practice with realistic AI outputs including errors, builds both skill and trust. Microlearning modules enable spaced repetition across busy schedules. Post-training assessments, ticket analysis, and user satisfaction surveys provide data to iterate and improve the training program continuously.

question.en: What is the primary purpose of defining go/no-go criteria before an AI product launch?

text.en: To ensure the marketing campaign has a fixed launch date
To make launch decisions objective and threshold-based rather than driven by schedule pressure
To reduce the number of features included in the product
To transfer launch responsibility to the engineering team exclusively

explanation.en: Go/no-go criteria establish measurable, pre-agreed thresholds that remove subjectivity from launch decisions. This prevents the common failure mode of launching under deadline pressure despite unresolved risks, which can cause significant user harm and reputational damage.

question.en: Which AI-specific post-launch monitoring concern is unique to AI products and not typically tracked for conventional software releases?

text.en: Server uptime and availability
User login frequency
Model drift and confidence score degradation over time
Number of help documentation page views

explanation.en: Model drift — where an AI model's accuracy degrades as real-world data patterns shift away from training data — is a uniquely AI-specific risk. Conventional software does not degrade in this way, making it a critical post-launch monitoring dimension for AI products.

question.en: A product team conducts a 30-day post-launch retrospective and finds that activation rate is strong but feature adoption depth is very low. What is the most likely implication?

text.en: The AI model needs to be completely retrained
Users are discovering the product but not understanding or trusting its advanced features — pointing to a training or UX gap
The product should be immediately deprecated
The go/no-go criteria were set too strictly

explanation.en: High activation with low feature depth indicates users are entering the product but not engaging with its core AI capabilities. This pattern typically signals inadequate onboarding, unclear UX, or insufficient training — all addressable without a full product rebuild.
